title: Clay
strapline: Cold, heavy, endlessly changeable — real clay in real hands.
intent: Clay has a weight and resistance playdough never has: it pushes back, so hands and arms work hard and grow strong.
It holds whatever it's made into, so children can pursue a real idea — a pot, a face, a snail — and see it through.
Its cool, dense, malleable feel is deeply absorbing and calming, and draws in even reluctant children.
Working clay is full of rich process talk — pinch, roll, coil, smooth, press, join.
There is no 'right' outcome, so it's a safe place to have an idea, change it, and try again.
implementation: Use real clay, not just playdough — give it to children in generous lumps on boards, with water pots to smooth and join.
Sit and work alongside without making a model for them to copy — your absorbed hands are the invitation.
Name the actions as children discover them: 'You're rolling it into a long coil', 'You pressed your thumb right in.'
Offer simple tools sparingly — fingers first, then sticks, rollers, natural bits for printing into it.
Ask about the idea, not the result: 'Tell me about what you're making — what will it need next?'
Let children keep and dry their pieces, or squash and begin again — both are fine and both teach.
Have water and cloths ready so gloopy hands never cut the exploration short.
key_questions: How does the clay feel — how is it different from the playdough?
What are you making, and what does it need next?
How did you get it to do that — can you show me?
What could you use to make a mark or a pattern in it?
What will happen if you add a little water?

impact.text: Children pinch, roll, coil, press and join with increasing hand strength and fine control.
Children work towards their own idea and adapt it as they go, seeing a piece through.
Children explore the material deeply and repeatedly, testing what clay will and won't do.
Children use process words — roll, coil, smooth, join — to describe what their hands are doing.
Children become deeply, calmly absorbed, staying with the clay for long, focused stretches.
Children make marks and patterns in the clay with tools and natural objects.

enhancements: Water pots, slip and cloths for smoothing and joining.
Natural objects — shells, cones, twigs, leaves — to press and print into the clay.
Simple tools: rollers, blunt sticks, garlic press, textured mats.
A shelf to dry and display finished pieces, and a photo record of the process.
Small-world figures or beads to embed and build clay worlds around.
An outdoor clay dig or mud-and-clay area for large, messy, whole-arm work.

playing_exploring: Children explore a demanding, novel material with their whole hands and no fixed outcome.
They test it endlessly — what happens if I squeeze, roll, wet or press it?
active_learning: Children become deeply absorbed and persist with a tricky material and their own idea.
creating_thinking: Children form a plan, notice when it isn't working, and change their approach to make it happen.
